THE GRAND QUEST NOBODY GETS AROUND TO

Irreverents • Proposed narrative framework • 22 November 2026

# Core truth, already decided

The world sincerely believes it is caught in a momentous story with a real existential threat. The people who might be best able to help are profoundly distracted by everything else. They are not secretly destined to become obedient, nor must they eventually learn to care about the prophecy. Their behavior can be audacious, generous, criminal, destructive, brilliant, careless or heroic depending on whichever opportunity captures them.

The game's title, “Irreverents,” is NOT a name the party uses in the world. This is player-facing shorthand only.

# Proposed crisis: The Great Unbinding

The kingdom's ancient network of seals—stone sites, mirrors, archives, towers and strange mechanisms—keeps far-apart regions and dangerous things where they belong. Something powerful is breaking or exploiting that network. Unusual creatures emerge from old passages. Buildings fall out of alignment. Certain routes open for the first time in centuries; other routes become unstable. The king believes an ancient adversary is trying to unravel the foundations of civilization.

This is a WORKING PLOT OPTION, not approved canon. It is attractive because the crisis is tangible in the same exploratory world the party uses for more interesting pursuits. A “world-ending problem” is not just a dialogue claim: it causes new physical connections, threats and mysteries.

A theme may emerge: the official quest aims to restore the approved order, while the protagonists take pleasure in the new possibility. Avoid reducing the threat to “the villain is just trying to stop fun”; an antagonist should have sincere objectives independent of our joke.

# Alternative central threats (also unapproved)

A. THE SIEGE: an ancient sovereign is rebuilding an impossibly large army. Castles, cities and routes change as the invasion spreads. Familiar but direct; strong for mass combat and vehicle mayhem.

B. THE GREAT UNBINDING: broken seals make regions connect in unstable ways; boss-scale threats awaken and the world must choose what to keep shut. Strong for Amazing Mirror-like secrets and space.

C. THE LAST STORY: an ancient order tries to lock history into one inevitable “correct” narrative, closing off futures and possibilities. Rich thematic irony, but risk of being too self-referential or abstract.

Recommendation for exploration: start with B's concrete world behavior, borrow A's palpable adversarial pressure, and reserve C's philosophical texture as subtext rather than overt lecture.

# What the king thinks the main quest is

Proposed royal explanation: assemble or restore several sacred devices, consult the guardians of their sites, obtain the crown's blessing, march to the adversary's citadel and defeat the threat before the last seal breaks. The king has genealogy, precedent, charts, a sacred map and roughly three hours of mandatory historical context he is eager to give.

The player can follow this route. It should be a legitimate, satisfying series of extraordinary adventures in its own right. But it is only one route into the world, not the most privileged piece of content from a gameplay perspective.

# What the heroes notice instead

The king is seated in front of a stained-glass window over a long drop. The royal champion wears armor nobody has ever dented. A wizard has mysterious glowing pills. A captive dragon supposedly devastated the kingdom, and its restraints look improvable. A shelf might hide a passage. Someone has left the treasury door ajar. The party is fascinated by what these affordances invite, not by whether the king's ceremonial map is the “main quest.”

The opening is PLAYABLE. The speech does not reach a conventional end. After roughly three hours of listening it seamlessly becomes the actual credits—an absurd legitimate alternate ending. That feature is already owner-endorsed; any additional scene details here are proposals.

# Opening state, written for branching game logic

Player enters court. Speech starts in parallel with gameplay rather than taking over controls.

Objects that exist before trouble: champion armor and weapon; wizard's pocketed items; stained-glass window; caged dragon; suspicious wall; crown; chandelier mechanism; doors, guard patrols and low-level service rooms.

Player might simply leave with a quest clue. Or pickpocket the wizard and feed pills to dragon; free the beast; challenge champion; seize the crown; suplex king through the window; infiltrate the treasury; discover an underground passage; or wait three hours.

Each action updates local incident memory, NPC actions, faction reactions and access routes. They are not six forced choice buttons followed by six cinematics. Implementation may discretize outcomes, but must preserve freedom.

# The king as a recurring tragic-comedic figure

He is not necessarily stupid or malicious. He knows there is genuine catastrophe ahead. He takes his responsibilities seriously, has good reasons for fearing it and has prepared substantial plans. His recurring torment is that the heroes keep doing world-changing things while neglecting his briefing.

Example (tone only):

King: “When the seventh seal fails, the whole eastern frontier shall—”

Hero: “Is that armor really impervious?”

King: “To ordinary blades. But that is not the point!”

Hero: “Interesting. Where does he sleep?”

King: “I am attempting to explain the fate of the WORLD.”

Hero: “And I'm listening. But has anyone ever stolen it?”

The joke succeeds because the king means every word. Avoid making every adult in the kingdom a hapless buffoon.

# A villain whose dignity is always at risk

An adversary may work patiently for centuries on a terrifying campaign and expect a climactic duel. Instead, the protagonists keep stealing specialized weapons from sent assassins, racing one another through secret corridors or hijacking siege engines. The villain can be dangerous and clever while feeling profoundly insulted at being treated as a side attraction.

One proposed encounter: a terrifying envoy materializes mid-heist to deliver a formal ultimatum. The heroes are fascinated by the teleportation device and its possible access to a previously unreachable attic. They might defeat the envoy, bargain, steal the mechanism or simply ignore the warning.

Do not script this as their only encounter. The villains' machines and abilities should have game-system value outside boss fights.

# Proposed campaign structure (not an act-by-act mandate)

PHASE 1 — THE MISPLACED CHOSEN ONES. The royal opening teaches exploration by presenting more appealing options than exposition. First streets, forest branches, undercroft and local characters become accessible.

PHASE 2 — UNINTENDED HEROES. Player sees regional problems and uses powers to solve, worsen, exploit or ignore them. Towns develop contradictory feelings. The Hall begins to remember unusual feats.

PHASE 3 — CONSEQUENCES GET LARGE. The serious crisis spreads enough to create bigger opportunities: altered passages, powerful enemies, coveted machines, major faction mobilization, increasingly audacious heists and rescues.

PHASE 4 — THE MOST INTERESTING THING IN THE WORLD. The threat becomes a particularly epic object of curiosity. A major confrontation is available—but not forced and not the only remarkable thing on the map.

PHASE 5 — AFTER THE LEGEND. Whatever happened, world locations and their people react; some regions celebrate, others prosecute, and the party may continue finding secrets, pursuing heat or revisiting older routes.

These phases are ways to organize content pacing, not mandatory story chapters or linear unlocks.

# How story pressure should work without forced urgency

Hard timed apocalypse countdowns contradict the desired freedom to get distracted for hours. Consider pressure tied to meaningful player interaction or broad milestones, with gentle background evolution between them. A distant invasion can be visible and dangerous without making the world disappear if the party plays with local powers for thirty hours.

If the player never follows the quest, the world should still contain rich play. If a player accidentally damages a vital seal, the story should react. If they kill a major named figure, favor replacement leadership, faction conflict or improvised response over an arbitrary “essential NPC” shield, within production limits.

This raises implementation questions; it is not permission to promise infinite reactive authored story branches.

# Player interaction with the sacred story

The player might voluntarily repair a seal because a broken mechanism threatens a beloved location.

The player might break a seal deliberately to summon a truly formidable opponent.

The player might steal sacred objects for unrelated practical use.

The player might rescue a guardian to gain a character recruit, then forget the guardian's mission.

The player might kill or befriend a supposed antagonist long before the main quest expects it.

The player might reach a crisis site through an undercroft shortcut while completely unaware of the intended royal map.

The game should recognize the consequences rather than merely checking a canonical mission-completion order.

# Endings as outcomes rather than commands

A straightforward save-the-world ending should be legitimate. So might an ambiguous stabilization, a catastrophic failure, an accidental victory, the heroes leaving to do something else, or the three-hour speech credits.

Not all endings have to be equally developed, and the exact set is undecided. What matters is the architecture of a story that can survive being ignored or undermined.

Avoid telling the player that their choice was morally “wrong” because it deviated from the main plot.

# Three storytelling tools

A. INTERRUPTION. The dramatic speech continues while the world provides affordances; the player chooses the focal point.

B. CONSEQUENCE. People, places and factions react concretely to whatever they did; this is how the world tells the story.

C. COMMEMORATION. The Hall records extraordinary episodes without dictating their moral interpretation. The record may be more famous than the intended main quest.

# Dialogue tone and comic rhythm

Straight-faced seriousness beats nonstop quipping. Comedy comes from sincere institutions meeting irresistible opportunity.

Proposed lines, not final script:

“The royal advisor has specifically requested that you do not touch the dragon again.”

“By royal decree you are barred from the treasury, unless the enemy army returns, in which case please report to the east gate.”

“Your Majesty, the heroes have returned.” / “Wonderful!” / “They're standing on the roof of the vault.” / “Not wonderful.”

“Champion, nobody has ever lifted you before!” / “He has not \*lifted\* me. This is an administrative error.”

Never force dialogue that pre-judges which action the player will choose.

# What must remain unresolved

Exact antagonist, cosmology, kingdom names, number of sacred seals, final quest structure, optionality of endings, consequences of killing major characters, and how time advances must be selected through review and prototyping. The completed game should be commercially and technically coherent without destroying its irreverent premise.

PRIORITY OVERRIDE — NEW WORLD PREMISE, 22 NOV 2026

Read before selecting any candidate villain or plot: the owner has specified a world that has made the HERO'S JOURNEY a de facto religion. EVERYONE passionately wants all events to fit the EXPECTED GLORIOUS MAIN QUEST EXACTLY; characters are SUPER TYPECAST and things are for precisely their obvious sacred purpose. This replaces weaker framing that the world merely enjoys heroic stories, or reinterpretations that automatically make every unexpected action part of destiny. The culture must be maximally sincere and predictable; the PLAYERS are the source of creative discontinuity. The crisis proposed as “The Great Unbinding” and all detailed lore remain speculative, and any selected crisis should reinforce this contrast rather than make every NPC too flexible or meta-aware.
